request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Front-desk receptionist, female, 3rd year

Interviewer: The hotel switched to a new front-desk system this year. How have you found it?

Interviewee: The new system was rolled out across the whole group. At the training, the instructor said it would raise efficiency by thirty percent. At first I didn’t really believe it. I thought it was just the official line, because when has changing systems ever been painless? Two months in, it really is a lot faster. Checking someone in used to mean switching back and forth between three screens; now it’s all done on one. You scan the guest’s ID card and the details fill in automatically, and the deposit can be paid by scanning a code. Guests spend much less time standing at the desk, and we don’t have to keep apologising while we wait for pages to load. Once last month a tour group arrived, more than forty people coming into the lobby at once. Before, they’d have queued for at least half an hour. That day, a colleague and I checked them all in within twenty minutes, and the tour leader came over specially to say thank you. I used to copy out the reservations by hand every day when I started my shift, in a hardcover notebook I bought myself, because I was afraid of making mistakes. That notebook has been sitting in my drawer untouched for ages now. The system flags duplicate names, overbooking and insufficient deposits automatically, and checks more carefully than I did myself, so we don’t have to go through the notebook at handover any more either. Our night-shift colleagues say the night audit takes almost an hour less than before, so they can hand over and go home earlier, and if there’s a problem they call the support hotline and someone gets back to them within ten minutes. Last week the manager showed us the figures: the average queuing time went down from eight minutes to five. The interface also looks better than the old one: the colours and icons are all very clear. Honestly, I really do think switching systems was the right call this time.
